notes:
I've put these notes together from the pages my searches returned. A few gaps are listed at the end.

## Luke 18:1–22: Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1:**
- Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic): Jesus didn't mean we should always be kneeling with our eyes closed. He meant we should always be in "the spirit of prayer," which matches Paul's "pray without ceasing." i. Jesus did not mean that we should always have our knees bent and eyes closed in prayer; but we must always be in what is sometimes called *the spirit of prayer*. Paul mentioned this idea in 1 Thessalonians 5:17 when he wrote, *pray without ceasing*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- A different reading: MacArthur, quoted on Precept Austin, says this isn't a general call to prayer. He calls it "eschatological prayer": praying for the Lord to come and for strength to last until he does. So this is not a call to prayer in general like, "Pray without ceasing."  That's a call to unceasing prayer in general. This is a call to eschatological prayer, pray that the Lord will come and pray for the strength to endure until He arrives, to endure the flesh, the world, the devil, the hostility against the gospel, persecution, rejection, and even martyrdom. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-18-commentary)
- Clarke (Methodist): he links the verse to the troubles about to come on the land, which would call for patience and constant prayer. that as afflictions and desolations were coming on the land, and they should have need of much patience and continual fortitude, and the constant influence and protection of the Almighty, therefore they should be instant in prayer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-18.html)
- Geneva Notes (Reformed): God keeps us praying to train us, not to wear us out, so we have to resist impatience when answers are slow. God will have us to continue in prayer, not to weary us, but to exercise us; therefore we must fight against impatience so that a long delay does not cause us to quit our praying. (https://ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Luke/18.html)

**v. 2:**
- Geneva Notes: the parable argues from the lesser to the greater. If even a corrupt judge gives someone their due, the prayers of the godly will do far better with God. He does not compare things that are of equal stature, but the less with the greater: If a man receives what is rightfully his at the hands of a most unrighteous judge, much more will the prayers of the godly prevail before God. (https://ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Luke/18.html)
- Barclay: the judge can't have been a Jewish judge. Jewish disputes went to the elders, and a Jewish court needed three judges. (i) The judge was clearly not a Jewish judge. All ordinary Jewish disputes were taken before the elders, and not into the public courts at all. If, under Jewish law, a matter was taken to arbitration, one man could not constitute a court. There were always three judges, one chosen by the plaintiff, one by the defendant, and one independently appointed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-8.html)
- Barclay also says the parable contrasts God with the judge rather than comparing them. It does not liken God to an unjust judge; it contrasts him to such a person. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/luke-18.html)

**v. 3:**
- Pulpit Commentary: the widow stands for the church under pressure from an unbelieving world. Her plea is for relief from oppression, probably to get back an inheritance being kept from her, not for revenge. The forlorn woman of the parable represents the Church or people of God in dire straits, overborne by an unbelieving world and seemingly forgotten even of their God. all she wanted was that the judge should deliver her from the oppression which her adversary exercised over her, no doubt in keeping from her the heritage to which she was lawfully entitled. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/18.htm)
- Precept Austin: "saying" is in the present tense, so she kept on pressing her case. **Saying** is in the present tense which describes her continually presenting her her case to the ungodly judge. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-18-commentary)

**v. 4:**
- Bible.org (Utley): the judge "came to himself," much like the prodigal in Luke 15:17. In a sense this is similar to Luke 15:17. This judge had an epiphany; he came to himself. He began to realize the consequences of his decision. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21315)

**v. 5:**
- Utley: "wear me out" literally meant "to blacken one's eye." 18:5 "wear me out" This literally meant "to blacken one's eye" (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21315)
- Geneva Notes: the image comes from wrestlers or boxers hitting their opponents. Literally, "beat me down with her blows", and it is a metaphor taken of wrestlers who beat their adversaries with their fists or clubs (https://ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Luke/18.html)

**v. 6:**
- Benson (Methodist): if even shameless wicked men eventually respond to repeated cries, God will respond much more. If the repeated, importunate cries of the afflicted do at length make an impression on the hearts even of men so wicked as to glory in their impiety, injustice, and barbarity, they will much more be regarded by God (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-8.html)

**v. 7:**
- Guzik lists the contrasts: the judge was unfair and God is fair; the judge didn't care about the widow and God loves those who ask him. · The judge was unfair; God is fair. · The judge had no personal interest in the widow; God loves and cares for those who petition Him. He says delays are there to change us, not God. Yet the delays in prayer are not needed to change God, but to change us. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Pulpit Commentary takes "bear long" a different way: God is being patient with the oppressors, and that partly explains why answers are delayed. With the wrong-doers, whose works and words oppress and make life heavy and grievous to the servants of God; with these who have no claim to consideration will God bear long. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/18.htm)
- Wesley (Methodist) reads the verse historically: God vindicates Christians and saves them from the coming destruction of the Jewish nation. Preserve the Christians from all their adversaries, and in particular save them out of the general destruction, and avenge them of the Jews? (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/18.htm)
- Utley: the delay has a good purpose, such as the full number of the elect coming in. His delay has a beneficial purpose (i.e., full number of the elect, cf. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21315)

**v. 8:**
- Pulpit Commentary: "speedily" means suddenly rather than soon, like a thief in the night. It means that God will act in accordance with his servant's prayer, not soon, but suddenly (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/18.htm)
- Wesley's comment, via StudyLight: whenever Christ appears, there will be how few true believers will be found upon earth! (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-8.html)
- Guzik: the faith Jesus will look for means knowing that God is not like the unjust judge and praying without losing heart. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)

**v. 9:**
- Guzik: trusting in your own righteousness and despising others go together almost inevitably. The connection between those who **trusted in themselves that they were righteous** and those who **despised others** is almost inevitable. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Wesley adds his own point: the Pharisee was not a hypocrite but was sincere in his self-trust. the Pharisee here mentioned was no hypocrite, no more than an outward adulterer: but he sincerely trusted in himself that he was righteous (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/18.htm)
- Geneva Notes: two things empty prayer of its value, confidence in our own righteousness and contempt for others. Two things especially make our prayers void and of no effect: confidence of our own righteousness, and our contempt of others (https://ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Luke/18.html)

**v. 10:**
- Utley: the Pharisee was known for sincere devotion, and the tax collector was an outcast and a friend of Rome. The first was noted for his sincere religiosity and commitment to doing God's will. The second was known as a social outcast, friend of Rome, and totally ostracized from the religious community of Israel (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21315)

**v. 11:**
- Guzik: the Pharisee was really praying to himself and said "I" five times. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: being kept from gross sins was a real reason to thank God, but the Pharisee used it to set himself above everyone else. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/luke-18.html)
- Coffman: the prayer was a monologue that admitted no need and asked for no mercy. The prayer of the Pharisee was a monologue, acknowledging no need, seeking no blessing, confessing no lack, admitting no sin, and beseeching no mercy (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-18.html)

**v. 12:**
- Wesley: strict Pharisees fasted every Monday and Thursday, and many gave a second tenth as alms. He sums up the plea as I do no harm: I use all the means of grace: I do all the good I can. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/18.htm)
- Utley: the tithing itself wasn't wrong. The problem was the attitude behind it. It is not that his tithing was inappropriate. It was the attitude behind the tithe ("of all") that turns this into self-righteousness instead of devotion. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21315)

**v. 13:**
- Guzik: the word for "have mercy" relates to atoning sacrifice. The prayer amounts to "be satisfied with the atoning sacrifice, and forgive me." He prayed, "O God, be satisfied with the atoning sacrifice, and forgive me." He also cites Barclay that the Greek reads "*the* sinner." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Expositor's Greek Testament: the tax collector stands apart out of a strong sense that he deserves nothing, not out of pride. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/luke-18.html)
- Wesley: he stood far from the holy of holies, held back by shame. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/18.htm)

**v. 14:** This is where traditions differ most.
- **Reformed (Calvin):** this isn't a matter of degree. The tax collector was accepted and the Pharisee was rejected. The verse shows that "justified" means standing before God as if righteous. Christ does not merely assign to *the publican* a certain degree of superiority, as if *righteousness* had belonged alike to both, but means that*the publican* was accepted by God, while *the Pharisee* was totally rejected. And this passage shows plainly what is the strict meaning of the word *justified:* it means, to stand before God as if we were righteous. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-14.html)
- **Gill (Baptist):** "rather than the other" doesn't mean the Pharisee was partly justified. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/18-14.html)
- **Guzik:** the justification was immediate, with no trial period. He didn't earn his justification, and he didn't have a probationary period; he was simply **justified**. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- **Wesleyan:** Wesley reads "rather than the other" as "and not the other." justified rather than the other - That is, and not the other. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/18.htm) Coffman's Restoration Movement commentary stresses humility as the deciding factor. Humility is taught, a virtue which is so important that all of the goodness of the Pharisee could not save him without it, and all of the shame and unworthiness of the publican could not condemn him as long as he had it. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/luke-18.html)
- **Older scholarly caution:** the Expositor's Greek Testament says the word is Pauline but not necessarily used in Paul's sense here; it may simply mean "pardoned." δεδικαιωμένος , justified (here only in Gospels), a Pauline word, but not necessarily used in a Pauline sense = pardoned. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/egt/luke-18.html)
- **Precept Austin** applies the second half of the verse to eternal destinies: self-exaltation ends in judgment. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-18-commentary)

**v. 15:**
- Benson: this story fittingly follows the parable, because it confirms that God accepts the humble. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-15.htm)
- Cambridge Bible: Jewish mothers seem to have carried their babies to eminent rabbis for a blessing. It seems to have been a custom of Jewish mothers to carry their babes to eminent Rabbis for their blessing (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-15.htm)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the disciples thought infants couldn't receive anything from Jesus. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-15.htm)

**vv. 15–17: infant baptism** (a real disagreement between traditions)
- **Reformed (Calvin):** he uses this passage "as a shield against the Anabaptists." Since baptism is the pledge of forgiveness and adoption, he argues it shouldn't be denied to infants whom God adopts. it is not without reason that we employ this passage as a shield against the Anabaptists. (https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment2/v1.0/harry/comm_vol32/htm/ii.lxix.htm) The Geneva Notes say the elect children of believers are included in God's free covenant. (https://ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/Luke/18.html)
- **Baptist:** Gill says the passage never mentions baptism and doesn't imply it. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-15.htm) Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: "He did not baptize them, but he did bless them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/) Steven Cole on Bible.org quotes Spurgeon saying one could as easily prove vaccination from this text. Cole sees the passage as support for dedicating children and leading them to faith later. The text does provide warrant for publicly dedicating children to Christ and for leading them to personal faith in Christ when they're old enough to understand. (https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-83-bringing-children-jesus-luke-1815-17)
- **Lutheran:** I found no Lutheran source on this passage. A sermon by MacArthur (Baptist) describes Lutheran teaching from outside and argues against it. (https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-369/Is-Infant-Baptism-Biblical?Term=infant)

**v. 16:**
- Guzik: children love to come to Jesus, so we should never block their way. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- Matthew Henry: none are too young to be brought to Christ. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/18-16.htm)

**v. 17:**
- Pulpit Commentary: children never claim merit, and the previous parable was still on Jesus' mind. Jesus here reminds men that if they hope to enter the kingdom, it must be in the spirit of children, who never think of putting forward any claim of merit or paying any price for kindness showed them. His late parable of the Pharisee and publican was evidently in the Master's mind when he said this. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/18.htm)
- Bob Deffinbaugh on Bible.org: babies don't do anything; they are carried to Jesus. (https://bible.org/seriespage/blessed-babes-and-miserable-millionaire-luke-1815-30)

**v. 18:**
- Pulpit Commentary suggests the man was a member of the council, the noblest kind of Pharisee. His question concerning eternal life indicates that he was a Pharisee, and he evidently represented the noblest phase of this religious party. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/18.htm)
- MacArthur instead sees him as a wealthy layman, probably the leader of a synagogue. (https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/41-51/the-blasphemy-of-the-rich-young-ruler)
- Precept Austin: his question was about "doing," the opposite of receiving the kingdom like a child (v. 17). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-18-commentary)

**v. 19:**
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: either Jesus was good or he shouldn't be called good, and since only God is good, Jesus must be God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- GotQuestions: Jesus wasn't denying he was divine; he was pushing the man to think about what "good" really means. (https://www.gotquestions.org/rich-young-ruler.html)

**v. 20:**
- GotQuestions: Jesus wasn't offering salvation by keeping the law. He was holding up the law as God's perfect standard. In telling the young man to keep the commandments, Jesus was not saying that he could be saved by obeying the commandments; rather, Jesus was emphasizing the Law as God's perfect standard. (https://www.gotquestions.org/rich-young-ruler.html)
- Leon Morris, quoted on Precept Austin: taking the law seriously starts a person on the way to Christ. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-18-commentary)
- **Catholic view:** the Catholic Encyclopedia reads "keep the commandments" (Matthew's version) as truly enough for eternal life. That was all that was necessary in the strict sense of the word, and by thus keeping the commands which God had given eternal life could be obtained. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04435a.htm)

**v. 21:**
- Guzik: he may really have kept them outwardly, blameless in the eyes of men like Paul in Philippians 3:6. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/)
- MacArthur: he broke the first table of the law by having another god. (https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/41-51/the-blasphemy-of-the-rich-young-ruler)

**v. 22:** Readings differ here.
- **Protestant (Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal):** the command was a test aimed at this man, not a rule for everyone. Sproul: Jesus did not set down a rule that everybody must embrace poverty to be His follower. He links it to the first commandment. (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/rich-young-ruler-luke18) Guzik says riches had become this man's idol, and that it's also wrong to think the command applies to no one. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-18/) Piper (Desiring God) sees "follow me" as the heart of it, with Jesus meant to be the man's supreme treasure. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/remember-the-rich-young-man)
- **Catholic:** this is an "evangelical counsel" of voluntary poverty for those seeking perfection, not a precept for all. it is possible to be rich, and married, and held in honour by all men, and yet keep the Commandments and to enter heaven. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04435a.htm) Augustine likewise calls selling all a "greater" precept beyond the commandments. (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/160335.htm)
- **Prosperity vs. "poverty gospel":** Guzik describes both camps. Poverty-gospel advocates point to this verse, and prosperity advocates point to rich, godly people in the Bible. His own conclusion is that Jesus clearly called riches an obstacle to the kingdom. Clearly Jesus said that *riches are an obstacle to the kingdom of God*. (https://enduringword.com/did-jesus-preach-a-prosperity-gospel-or-a-poverty-gospel-live-qa-for-september-12-2024-2/)

## What I couldn't find
- Notes from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, so the modern-scholarship view is thin. The Expositor's Greek Testament remark on v. 14 is the nearest thing I have.
- Any Orthodox (oca.org) source.
- A Catholic source on justification in v. 14.
- Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Pentecostal (ag.org, pneumareview.com) sources written in their own voice.
- Commentary specifically on the faith in v. 8 from a word-of-faith or hyper-grace angle.
